newsitem.title: USA: U.S. inflation seen mostly tame near-term - experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. inflation seen mostly tame near-term - experts.

text.p: U.S. inflation is mostly tame and is expected to remain that way in the near future.
Although some pressures may lurk at the margins, Wall Street pundits said an in-depth look at the current cycle hints the inflation jitters will likely prove unfounded.
"I think ... inflation is not a major threat," said Richard Berner, executive vice president and chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp.
"What we're seeing here are some cyclical pressures that are likely to translate in an almost imperceptible worsening in inflation," he added.

The "cyclical pressures" were more evident last week, when some private retail sales indicators showed consumer spending might be on the rise and oil prices surged on renewed military unrest in Kurdish areas in northern Iraq.
Although rising oil could cause problems, analysts said the situation now is less threatening than last spring, when oil prices also jumped sharply.
"Rising oil prices is going to be the biggest problem but it's not going to be the same as in April," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.
"In September and October oil prices seasonally rise ... The seasonal (factors) are going to offset a lot of the increase that we've seen in the raw commodity price of oil."
Since September 23, the front-month crude oil contract traded in the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) has risen 10.8 percent to $25.90 a barrel at Friday's close.
On the consumption front, analysts said forecasts of stronger economic growth in the fourth quarter spurred by an increase in consumer demand offer little cause for alarm.
"You have to put this into perspective," Low said.

"Consumer spending will probably rise in the fourth quarter, but if you look at the rates of spending growth in the last couple of years, the stronger quarters posted increases of 3.5 or 4.0 percent. I don't think we're going to approach those levels now," he added.
He conceded retailers might do a little better, "but still, consumer spending is not going to be strong enough to allow price increases to be passed through."
Analysts also said a recent rise in food prices appears to be fading, which might as well contribute to a more stable overall inflation outlook.
Economists said the effects of poor harvests in the spring of 1996, which fueled inflation in prices of grains, poultry, meat and dairy products, seem to be abating.
"We had trouble with food prices, (but) this should be just about the end of it," Low said.
Economists said Americans have paid for the large meat and dairy increases that were visible in the overall September Consumer Price Index -- which rose 0.3 percent.

"But already in the (September) Producer Price Index we're beginning to see grain prices fall, wholesale prices for poultry are falling... So food prices are probably going to be a positive going forward," Low said.
But what about wage pressures? The picture seems mixed.
Some analysts, citing studies carried out by regional Federal Reserve Banks, said higher wages will not automatically translate into more inflation.

The San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank carried out a study last year which showed no correlation between U.S. wage growth and inflation. Also, the Dallas Fed did a study earlier this year that showed similar results.

"These studies have drawn on other studies done by private sector economists .. It's very hard to find any correlation, any evidence that wages lead inflation. So I'm not particularly worried about it now," Low said.
But some economists said wage growth without a significant increase in productivity could be a source of concern.

"Productivity growth has been under one percent a year so that does imply some upward pressure on the unit labor cost, which tends to be reasonably closely correlated with inflation," said David Sloan, senior economist at consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc.
On average, analysts predict overall CPI inflation is likely to stay somewhere between 3.0 and 3.4 percent in 1996, against 2.7 percent seen last year.
